## Investigación con agentes (Claude Opus 5.5; puede contener errores)
# Research notes: federal suit over the Texas DPS voter-registration transmission failure (as of Oct 5, 2026)

**Bottom line:** As of Oct 5, 2026, none of the three research agents found a qualifying filing. There is no new federal complaint, no motion to enforce the 2021 Stringer settlement, and no state-court suit over the October 2025 error. The only legal step so far is a July 2026 demand letter from the Texas Civil Rights Project (TCRP) and the League of Women Voters of Texas. A demand letter does not count for resolution. The Secretary of State (SOS) answered in writing that it "stand[s] ready to vigorously contest your allegations." Ten days remain before the Oct 15, 2026 deadline.

## 1. What the resolution sources show (checked Oct 5, 2026)

- **Democracy Docket Texas page** (https://www.democracydocket.com/cases/?state=texas): no listed case concerns DPS transmission, Stringer, motor-voter or the NVRA.
  - The newest entry is Peoples v. Tarrant County (polling-place closures), filed Oct 2, 2026.
  - The 2026 entries are LULAC v. Nelson (the excluded SAVE purge suit, filed Mar 26, 2026, after an NVRA notice on Jan 15, 2026), Coleman v. Adams (Mar 3), NFB of Texas v. Hudspeth (Feb 3) and Houston Justice v. Harris County (Jan 25).
  - The page renders with JavaScript. The first fetch failed and the second returned this list, so treat it as reasonably reliable rather than certain.
- **Democracy Docket's page for the original Stringer case** (https://www.democracydocket.com/cases/texas-dmv-voter-registration/): status "Decided/Victory." Its last activity is the August 2021 settlement and notice of compliance, with no 2025–26 entries.
- **Democracy Docket news alert, Sep 24, 2026** (https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/texas-election-workers-scramble-after-registration-snafu-leaves-thousands-off-voter-rolls/): mentions Stringer only as background and reports no litigation.
- **CourtListener docket for Stringer v. Hughs** (W.D. Tex. 5:20-cv-00046, https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/16693196/parties/stringer-v-hughs/): last entry Aug 3, 2021. The earlier case, 5:16-cv-257, was last updated Jan 15, 2021.
  - **Caveat:** CourtListener only shows uploaded filings, PACER was not reachable, and filings from the last few days may not be indexed.
- **Metaculus FAQ** (https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions): credible sources are reputable news organizations, official government sources and similar.

## 2. Recent news and current status

All of this is after the question opened (Oct 3, 2025) except the 2021 settlement, which is background, and the October 2025 vendor update, which is the event at issue.

- **Oct 2025:** A vendor software update truncated DPS batch records, dropping three data fields. The vendor is reported as Deloitte (Votebeat and Texas Tribune, Oct 1, 2026; CNBC, Oct 2, 2026). Deloitte's DPS contracts are reported at $84.46M.
- **Dec 2025–Feb 2026:** A separate, earlier glitch lost about 1,000 applications. State Sen. Donna Campbell's office flagged it on Mar 9, 2026, and DPS said it was fixed on Mar 10. This is not the same as the October 2025 error.
- **July 2026:** TCRP and the League of Women Voters wrote to DPS and the SOS.
  - They cited at least three affected voters and said the failures could violate the 2021 Stringer settlement and federal law.
  - **Unverified:** the exact date and wording, and whether the letter is a formal NVRA notice before a lawsuit.
- **Aug 2026:** The state replied.
  - DPS general counsel D. Phillip Adkins wrote that "occasional technical issues may arise."
  - SOS general counsel Adam Bitter wrote: "Your reliance on three purported instances across the State — out of 18 million registrants — is sorely misguided... should you choose to proceed with litigation on this matter, we stand ready to vigorously contest your allegations."
  - **Date conflict:** the agents date the SOS reply both Aug 6 and Aug 26, 2026.
  - Sources: https://www.texastribune.org/2026/10/01/texas-voter-registration-dps-secretary-state-2026-delay-dmv/ and https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/10/01/records-show-dps-knew-of-problems-with-texas-online-voter-registration-as-early-as-march/ (records show the agencies knew of portal problems in March 2026).
- **Late Aug 2026:** DPS traced the cause to the October 2025 update.
- **Sep 13, 2026:** DPS, the SOS and the vendor fixed the problem. **Sep 18:** the SOS confirmed it had received the records.
- **Sep 22, 2026:** State elections director Christina Adkins emailed the counties, and the story became public (https://www.texastribune.org/2026/09/22/texas-dps-voter-registration-applications-unsent/). The backlog went out to counties overnight Sep 22–23 (https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/09/23/dps-error-backlogged-voter-registration-applications-county-election-officials/).
- **Sep 23–26, 2026:** Calls for investigation from both parties.
  - Those calling included Democrats, state Rep. John Bucy, GOP state Sen. Paul Bettencourt, House Elections chair Matt Shaheen, U.S. Rep. Julie Johnson, and U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla, who wrote to Gov. Abbott and sought a federal probe (https://www.padilla.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/padilla-demands-answers-from-governor-abbott-on-texas-voter-registration-errors/).
  - Gov. Abbott's office called the issue "fully resolved," and the SOS offered grants to counties (https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2026/09/26/voter-registration-delay-backlog-online-dps-error/).
- **Sep 25, 2026:** The Tribune posted a letter to the governor, SOS and DPS whose author could not be identified (https://www.texastribune.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/9.25.26-Gov-SOS-DPS-VR-backlog.pdf).
- **Sep 30, 2026:** The SOS said provisional ballots will count if the DPS transaction is verified (https://www.fox7austin.com/election/texas-says-delayed-voter-registrations-will-be-processed-time). Tarrant County had processed about 81% of its 74,000 records.
- **Oct 2, 2026:** Democratic attorney general nominee Nathan Johnson vowed, if elected, to probe Deloitte (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/02/texas-ag-deloitte-voter-registration.html; read from search snippets only).
- **Oct 3, 2026:** Newsweek reported the state says the backlog is cleared and mentioned no litigation (https://www.newsweek.com/texas-clears-voter-backlog-as-advocates-warn-of-trust-concerns-12521286).

**How many were affected:** there is no official figure.
- Statewide estimates range from about 178,000 (Sen. Bettencourt, Sep 24) and at least 200,000 (Sep 26) to at least 500,000 records (Oct 1), with an unconfirmed estimate of up to 750,000.
- County figures: Harris about 75,000, Tarrant 74,000, Dallas 68,104, Collin 40,000+, Travis about 32,000–35,000.

**Advocacy groups:**
- TCRP is the most engaged; Sarah Chen and Karla Maradiaga have both criticized the state publicly. MOVE Texas and Common Cause have also commented; Common Cause wants the state to notify every affected voter.
- No group has announced an intent to sue.
- No statements found from ACLU of Texas, LULAC, MALDEF, Campaign Legal Center or Elias Law Group.

**Upcoming dates:**
- Oct 5, 2026: registration deadline.
- About Oct 19, 2026: early voting starts.
- Nov 3, 2026: Election Day.
- No legislative hearing found scheduled before Oct 15.

**Prediction markets:** none found.

## 3. Base rates and historical patterns

- **Stringer timeline** (sources: https://waterskraus.com/state-called-continuing-violate-federal-voter-law/ and https://my.lwv.org/texas/article/texas-voters-win-motor-voter-lawsuit-settled):
  - 2015: first notice to the state.
  - Mar 14, 2016: first suit filed, months after the notice.
  - Apr–May 2018: plaintiffs won in district court.
  - Late 2019: the 5th Circuit threw the case out on standing/mootness grounds.
  - Dec 19, 2019: new NVRA notice. Jan 14, 2020: Stringer v. Hughs refiled about 26 days later, probably using the 20-day rule before the March 2020 primary (inference).
  - Aug 28, 2020: the district court found NVRA violations; the 5th Circuit stayed that ruling.
  - Aug 2–3, 2021: settled. Texas will "permanently offer simultaneous voter registration" for online license renewals and updates.
  - **Unverified:** whether the court kept jurisdiction to enforce the settlement, and any monitoring terms or end date. If it did, a motion in 5:20-cv-46 could be filed quickly; if not, a new suit would be needed.
- **NVRA notice rules** (52 U.S.C. §20510(b)):
  - Normally plaintiffs must give notice and wait 90 days before suing.
  - The wait is 20 days if the violation occurs within 120 days of a federal election, and there is no notice requirement within 30 days of it. That no-notice window opened about Oct 4, 2026.
  - The July 2026 letter is more than 90 days old by October. Notice is therefore probably not a barrier to filing by Oct 15.
- **Mootness risk:** the system was fixed Sep 13 and the backlog delivered, which weakens the case for a suit. Mootness and standing are what sank the first Stringer suit in the 5th Circuit. A pre-election suit would likely seek narrow relief, such as making sure provisional ballots count or identifying applications that were never processed.
- **Similar glitches elsewhere** (rough synthesis, not exhaustive):
  - California DMV, 2018 (about 23,000 errors): no new suit. It was handled under an existing League of Women Voters/ACLU stipulated order, with audits and a 60-day report.
  - Georgia DDS, 2022 (automatic-registration rate fell from 79% to 39%): a request for a DOJ investigation, no federal suit found (low-to-medium confidence).
  - Arizona MVD, 2024 (about 218,000 voters): found Sep 6, petition filed in the Arizona Supreme Court Sep 17, ruled Sep 20. State court only, no federal suit.
  - Pattern: discrete glitches that were already fixed mostly led to letters, audits, inquiries, or action under existing court orders, not new federal suits. Systemic suits under the NVRA's motor-voter section (§5) usually come weeks to months after a notice. Stringer II's 26 days is the fast end.
- **Texas litigation tempo:** TCRP, the League of Women Voters of Texas, MOVE Texas and the Democratic committees often sue within weeks of a triggering event: the 2020 mail-ballot and drop-box suits, Stringer II, and the 2026 SAVE suit (about 10 weeks from notice). Working the other way, courts avoid changing election rules close to an election (the *Purcell* principle), and the 5th Circuit stayed Stringer quickly in 2020.

**Still unverified:**
- The exact date and text of the July 2026 letter.
- The Stringer settlement's enforcement and jurisdiction terms.
- Any filings after about Oct 2–3, 2026.

**Worth checking before Oct 15:** PACER for 5:20-cv-46, press pages for TCRP and the League of Women Voters of Texas, the Democracy Docket Texas page in a browser, and Texas Tribune and Votebeat coverage.

criterios: This question resolves YES if, as of 23:59 US Central Time on October 15, 2026, a new lawsuit has been filed in a United States federal district court whose primary claims concern the Texas Department of Public Safety's (DPS) failure to transmit online voter-registration applications/updates to the Texas Secretary of State and county registrars (the data-transmission error attributed to an October 2025 third-party vendor software update and remediated in September 2026). The suit must have been initiated on or after October 3, 2025; it may name DPS, the Texas Secretary of State, or related state officials as defendants, and may be a standalone complaint or a motion to enforce the 2021 Stringer v. Hughs settlement filed in federal court. It resolves NO otherwise. Resolution will be based on the case listings on Democracy Docket's Texas page (https://www.democracydocket.com/cases/?state=texas), reporting by the Texas Tribune, or other [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).
letra_pequena: A pre-litigation demand letter, a request for a government investigation, an administrative complaint, or a filing solely in a Texas state court does not count. The separate federal lawsuit over Texas's use of the SAVE database to flag voters for removal (filed March 2026) does not count, because its primary claims concern voter-roll removals rather than the DPS transmission failure; a suit whose primary claims are about voter-roll removals, purges, or other matters does not qualify merely because it mentions the DPS transmission error in passing. If a qualifying suit cannot be confirmed through the listed sources, the question resolves NO.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About 10 days, until 23:59 US Central Time on October 15.

(b) **Status quo:** NO. As of October 5, the research found demand letters and calls for investigation, but no qualifying federal filing.

(c) **Reference class:** In the three comparable voter-registration glitches identified by the research, none produced a new federal suit over the glitch. That is a small, imperfect sample, but it supports a low base rate for a filing within the next 10 days.

(d) **NO scenario:** Counties finish processing the corrected records, advocates monitor affected voters, and any remaining disputes are handled without a federal filing by the deadline.

(e) **YES scenario:** After the registration deadline, advocates identify voters whose applications still have not been processed and promptly file a federal complaint or seek to enforce the Stringer settlement.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** A motion to enforce the 2021 settlement in federal court **does** count; a demand letter, investigation request, or state-court filing does not. A qualifying filing must also be confirmable through the specified credible sources.

The election creates urgency, and the prior demand letter gives advocates a head start. Still, the reported fix and the absence of a filing so far make NO substantially more likely.

(a) **Time left:** About 10 days, until 23:59 CT on October 15, 2026.

(b) **Status quo:** No federal suit and no motion to enforce Stringer has been filed. Only a July 2026 demand letter and calls for investigations exist. If nothing changes, the answer is NO.

(c) **Reference class:** Discrete DMV/DPS registration-transmission glitches that were found and fixed before an election.
- California 2018 and Georgia 2022 led to no new federal suit.
- Arizona 2024 went to state court only.
- New federal NVRA suits usually come weeks to months after the trigger, if at all.
- The base rate for a new federal suit within about a month of public disclosure, after the fix, is roughly 5–15%.

(d) **NO scenario:** The backlog has been delivered and counties finish processing. The Secretary of State's guidance that provisional ballots will count if the DPS transaction is verified takes away the urgent pre-election harm. The Texas Civil Rights Project and League of Women Voters keep monitoring, gather affected voters, and perhaps sue after the election, when mootness and *Purcell* concerns are weaker. Or the matter stays with legislative and political investigations.

(e) **YES scenario:** Advocates find voters who were wrongly left off the rolls or whose records are still unprocessed after the October 5 deadline. The Texas Civil Rights Project, League of Women Voters or Democratic committees then file an emergency suit in the Western District of Texas, or a motion to enforce the Stringer settlement. They ask for notice to affected voters, extended processing, or a guarantee that provisional ballots count. No pre-suit notice is required within 30 days of the election, and the state's letter explicitly invited litigation.

(f) **Technicalities:**
- The suit's primary claims must concern the DPS transmission failure.
- A filing in state court does not count.
- A motion to enforce Stringer filed in federal court does count, but only if the court kept jurisdiction over the settlement, which is unverified.
- The filing must be confirmable through credible sources by October 15.
- A suit filed late on October 14–15 might not be reported in time.

The fix and the state's provisional-ballot assurance reduce the incentive to sue, though the large scale of the backlog (hundreds of thousands of records) and the active advocacy groups keep a non-trivial tail.

Probability: 9%
